title: Eviction latency SLA tradeoffs and prefetch governor (draft)
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes on the tradeoffs between aggressive eviction (to bound memory residency) and tail latency SLA when prefetching is used as a mitigation. This is a synthesis of lab runs from 2025-02-20 -> 2025-03-01 and hypotheses for a light-weight prefetch governor to reduce p95/p99 spikes without blowing up bandwidth.

Background / motivation:
- We’ve seen cases where tenant-level memory caps trigger aggressive eviction spikes (e.g., when many long-seqlen requests arrive). That reduces resident set but increases page faults and NVMe spillback reads which can cause p95/p99 latency spikes.
- Prefetching (predictive warm-up of KV pages) reduces misses but can oversubscribe memory and read bandwidth, causing degraded tail latency on the whole GPU host during concurrent workloads.
- We need a governor that trades off prefetching aggressiveness based on observed memory pressure and active bandwidth usage, to keep tail latency within SLA while maintaining reasonable reuse.

Test matrix (summary):
- Hardware: 2x A100-80GB hosts in staging (single-socket NUMA mapping), NVMe local read latency ~120–200us under moderate IO; PCIe/NVLink topology unchanged.
- Workloads: mixed multi-tenant traces: 60% short-chat (avg seqlen 64), 30% medium (256), 10% long (1024). Injected hotkey surges at t=600s.
- Variables: eviction aggressiveness (conservative/moderate/aggressive), prefetch policy (none, static prefetch X pages, adaptive governor), reservation window size (slot-based 1s/5s), pinning enabled/disabled.
- Observed signals (collected at host level): KV miss rate, reuse rate (sampled over 1m windows), NVMe bandwidth utilization, GPU mem usage, host CPU stalled IO waits, p50/p95/p99 token generation latency.

Key observations from runs:
1) Aggressive eviction + no prefetch:
- Reuse rate dropped ~35% vs baseline.
- NVMe read tail increased (many small reads), NVMe bandwidth lower (read amplification), p99 latency increased by ~3x during hotkey surges.
- Good steady-state memory headroom but poor tail SLA.

2) Aggressive eviction + static prefetch (fixed 32 pages on miss):
- Reuse recovered partially (+18% vs no prefetch), p95 improved but p99 still bad during concurrent surges.
- NVMe bandwidth shot up to ~92% during learning periods, causing background IO queueing and elevating host-level IO latency. Net effect: tail latency improved for prefetch recipients but other tenants suffered.

3) Moderate eviction + adaptive prefetch governor (bandwidth-aware):
- Reuse recovered ~+30% vs baseline without blowing memory caps.
- Prefetch governor limited bandwidth usage to ~70% of measured NVMe bandwidth; when host bandwidth >75% the governor backs off prefetch rate and prioritizes direct miss reads.
- Result: p95 reduced by ~22%, p99 reduced by ~38% relative to the aggressive/no-prefetch baseline. No large host-wide IO queueing observed.

4) Conservative eviction + aggressive prefetch:
- Highest reuse (~+45%) but memory headroom small; occasional out-of-memory (OOM) reclamations when multiple tenants prefetch simultaneously. p99 improved for affected requests but global tail suffered intermittently.

Telemetry highlights (representative numbers):
- Baseline reuse rate (no prefetch, moderate eviction): 61% sampled-resuse-over-1m
- Aggressive eviction reuse rate: 39%
- Static prefetch reuse rate: ~57% but NVMe BW = 90–95% peak
- Adaptive governor reuse rate: 53–60% with NVMe BW capped ~68–75% (adaptive across runs)
- p50 latency across runs: stable ~18–23ms per token
- p95 latency: 90ms -> 230ms depending on config; governor runs ~70–110ms
- p99 latency: 240ms -> 1.0s; governor runs ~150–400ms

Hypotheses / interpretation:
- The main driver for p99 blowups is NVMe queueing created by bulk prefetch reads combined with microbursts of misses during hotkey transitions. Bulk prefetch without awareness of current IO utilization shifts latency from individual misses to global queueing latency.
- Purely reducing eviction aggressiveness is not an operational solution: memory headroom is finite and some tenants need strict caps. We must instead reduce the IO impact of prefetching.
- An adaptive governor that takes two signals (host NVMe bandwidth utilization and current resident-set headroom) can provide most of the reuse benefit while avoiding IO amplification.

Design sketch: prefetch governor (v0):
- Inputs: instantaneous NVMe read BW (smoothed 2s EMA), current host mem headroom (GB free), local eviction pressure metric (% of eviction events in last 30s), request priority (system vs best-effort).
- Controls: prefetch budget per-request (pages to prefetch), prefetch concurrency cap, prefetch throttle (ms spacing between page fetch ops).
- Policy rules (priority-ordered):
  1) If NVMe BW > 80% -> disable prefetch for best-effort tenants, limit system tenants to 1 page per miss.
  2) If eviction pressure > threshold (e.g., >30% of slots reclaimed) -> reduce prefetch page count by 50% and increase spacing.
  3) When running in low-BW (<50%) and headroom > X GB -> allow aggressive prefetch up to N pages.
  4) For long-running requests with known hot windows (based on past seq history) allow opportunistic background prefetch when host idle.

Small experiments to validate governor knobs cheaply:
- Run A: enable governor with NVMe BW thresholds 75/50 for RBAC tiers; measure p99 and reuse.
- Run B: introduce prefetch spacing of 5ms vs 20ms and compare IO queue depth.
- Run C: add per-tenant token-bucket for prefetch concurrency to avoid synchronized prefetch storms.

Operational considerations / telemetry to add:
- Add metric: prefetch-induced read backlog (reads/sec attributable to prefetch vs reads/sec on-demand).
- Expose governor state in trace spans (why prefetch was throttled/backed off).
- Per-tenant prefetch budget and recent prefetch debt for accountability in Dedicated.

Risks / failure modes:
- Under-estimating available NVMe bandwidth on certain instances -> governor too conservative -> lost reuse, higher cost. Mitigate: calibrate per-instance baseline during startup.
- Overly aggressive global caps may starve system-critical warmups (e.g., model compilation or cold KV population). Use tenant priority exceptions with verification.
- Telemetry lag can cause oscillation if EMA windows are too short. Use conservative smoothing and hysteresis.

Next steps / action items (owner -> assignee):
- (Maya) Land a lightweight governor prototype behind feature flag + instrumentation in staging. (JIRA:INF-4872)
- (Arjun) Add prefetch-read attribution metrics and governor state to traces. (JIRA:INF-4920)
- (Liam) Run staged A/B test against mixed-traces for 48h and collect p50/p95/p99 and NVMe BW histograms.
- (Sofia) Draft runbook: when to disable prefetch per host and how to interpret prefetch-debt alarms.

Unresolved questions:
- What is the right per-tenant prefetch budget for Dedicated customers with strict SLA guarantees? (should be configurable per-contract)
- Should we implement a bank-aware prefetch that spreads reads across NVMe/PCIe queues to reduce hot-queueing? (likely helpful, needs deeper IO stack analysis)

Notes to self / scribbles:
- Related: INF-3218 was the earlier prefetch experiment that used static windowing; lessons learned there (esp. on prefetch concurrency) are still relevant.
- Verify behavior on multi-socket hosts where PCIe lanes map unevenly to NVMe controllers. Governor needs awareness of per-controller BW.

Bottom line:
- Static prefetching improves reuse but can catastrophically increase host-wide tail latency via IO queueing. An adaptive, bandwidth-aware prefetch governor with tenant-aware budgets looks promising: it recovers much of the reuse benefit and mostly avoids p99 blowups. Prototype + staged A/B test are the immediate next steps.

Appendix: quick run notes (timestamps):
- 2025-02-20 09:12 run-A aggressive-evict-no-prefetch: hotkey surge @600s -> p99 spike to 1.03s, NVMe read latency median 190us, read BW 38GB/s peak (queueing visible)
- 2025-02-22 13:05 run-B static-prefetch-32: prefetch caused read BW 47GB/s peak (sustained 90% of device), p95 improved but cross-tenant p99 increased to 860ms
- 2025-02-26 11:30 run-C adaptive-gov-v1: BW kept <=72%, p99 ~320ms at worst, reuse 57%

If you want I can convert the run logs into a compact CSV for quick plotting or add a small sequence diagram for the governor logic.

-- Maya C.
